item.title: Ephemeral agents escape the Arrow Information Paradox
item.description:
The Arrow information paradox (AIP) says there's no ideal way for a potential buyer to determine the value (to them) of some private information a seller is offering to sell them, without actually receiving the information, thus jumping the gun on the potential trade.

The paradox happens because a sale of information is:

  • Irreversible: the information can't be "returned" like a physical good, once the cat's out of the bag
  • Indivisible: there's no sense in which "half a secret" can be half as valuable as the whole secret

In other words, if you're considering buying a huge amount of wine but you don't know the quality, you can sample a random bottle of the wine, and if the connoisseur who works for you says it's good you buy the whole lot. But if the thing you're considering buying is One Big Important Secret, you couldn't do something like this (at least in the pre-LLM era).

Of course, the way this has been dealt with in practice is NDAs. And patents I guess. But these only go so far, since they depend on a government to enforce the NDAs, and there have been exceptions where people broke NDAs for arguably justified reasons, e.g. whistleblowers. So in some cases the seller would still prefer to enforce the privacy by technical rather than legal means.

Why, fundamentally, has the AIP held? It's because (until recently) there has been no evaluator able to both:

  • Understand the secret information and make qualitative judgements about its value, in the buyer's specific context
  • Credibly forget everything about the secret information (or alternatively just vanish, removing the need for "forgetting")

Human evaluators can understand and exercise judgement but can't forget; cryptography (zero-knowledge proofs, confidential computing, etc.) can forget but can't judge.

Now, of course, over a billion people use competent agents—who can incorporate arbitrary context and make reliable qualitative judgements—on a weekly basis. These agents are also ephemeral, so you can get privacy guarantees you would only be able to get from a human evaluator by killing them.[1]

This is already a published idea called NDAI, not something I came up with. I just thought it was an interesting change in the state of affairs that more readers should be aware of.

Also, I note that an ephemeral agent can actually compute and report back to you a much wider variety of things than "what's the value of this information to me?" For example:

  • "does their private plan honor their public commitment?"
  • "is this an infohazard?"
  • "who had this idea first?"

(For the last one, note that a cryptographic hash can prove you had a certain exact string at a certain time, but you can't tell whether two separate hashed ideas are actually the same idea with just hashes. An ephemeral evaluator who can compare the plaintext unlocks that.)

Related reading

  • Arrow, K. (1962). “Economic Welfare and the Allocation of Resources for Invention.” In The Rate and Direction of Inventive Activity, NBER / Princeton University Press.
  • Rahaman, N., Weiss, M., et al. (2024). “Language Models Can Reduce Asymmetry in Information Markets.” arXiv:2403.14443
  • Stephenson, M., Miller, A., Sun, X., Annem, B., Parikh, R. (2025). “NDAI Agreements.” arXiv:2502.07924
  • Gooen, O. (2024). “LLM-Secured Systems: A General-Purpose Tool For Structured Transparency.” LessWrong.
  1. ^

    There's a technical detail here that for some levels of security what you actually want is an open-weights evaluator agent running in some kind of trusted environment, in order to close the gap of "whose computer is the agent running on?" There are also obvious concerns about the seller prompt-injecting the agent to ignore previous instructions and say their stuff is really valuable. So in a production-ready version of this you'd actually want to have a sophisticated setup where the buyer supplies their private context and instructions (which the seller doesn't get to see), the seller supplies the actual secret (which the buyer doesn't get to see), and everything runs in some kind of secure enclave so nobody sees all the private stuff together except the ephemeral agent.

item.title: Performative Neuroticism vs Genuine Connection
item.description:
It's Christmas. I'm seven years old. The unceasing cacophony of laughter around the dinner table subsides for a brief moment. I speak up and say something. Nobody reacts. Someone coughs. Then the silence is broken when somebody else cracks a witticism, and the uproar of laughter echoes around the house again, as joke after joke lets loose.

As I'm watching, observing, closely monitoring who says what, and what gets a reaction, subconsciously something dawns on me. When the next pause in the conversation arrives, this time I say something silly—and my family laughs! My uncle says, "Good one!" My grandfather shakes his head while smiling. My father nods approvingly. Then the moment passes, and I feel seen and loved.

Dinner after dinner, holiday after holiday, I intuit that love is what I'm seeking, and the currency to obtain it is jokes. Say something witty, and I get to feel seen and loved. Say something emotional or needy, and I get ignored.

Repeat this for twenty years, and you get a man who is an excellent charmer, storyteller, and comedian—truly refined in his craft of entertaining others. He learned that attention only comes when he's putting on a show, dazzling others with his intellect and wit. But, underneath it all, is a boy who just wants to feel seen and loved. Underneath it all, is a boy who's scared that if he were to let the mask down, that no one would love him.

I learned that it's easier to be liked, than it is to be loved.

It's strange, at age 27, to realize that what I've always perceived as one of my greatest strengths—my ability to capture and maintain attention from others—is also one of my biggest insecurities.

I wanted to explore this further, so I took to experimenting on myself.

In recent conversations, I decided to stop performing, to stop filling every pause with a joke, to stop saying smart things to impress people. Somatically, anxiety showed up immediately, squeezing my chest. Anxiety is often a marker for feeling unsafe.

But why am I feeling unsafe?

I contemplated this question for days, until I remembered what it was like growing up: family dinners and holidays where I learned that the only way to feel seen and loved was to be entertaining. If I'm not entertaining, then I'm nothing.

I know, from psychological research, that there’s often a negative emotion, like anxiety, underneath strong urges, pushing us to act a certain way. There are two common ways to deal with that neuroticism:

  1. Do nothing and continue to endure low-grade chronic anxiety.
  2. Confront the insecurity and feel intense anxiety through multiple uncomfortable exposures, until eventually your nervous system habituates and you can relax.

I took the second option. While I desperately want to be in control of every social situation, I started letting breathing room exist in conversations. My anxiety quickly spiked, urging me to fill the space, but I repeatedly refused to react and instead just sat through the discomfort. And then, something interesting happened…


People began opening up to me. The extra space gave them time to think, reflect on what they were saying, and then add more if they wanted to. As people began trusting me and letting me into their inner worlds, I slowly started letting people into my inner world. Rather than desperately needing to be liked by compulsively entertaining people, I started feeling more genuinely connected to them and curious about their experiences. 

Something in my chest expanded.

In conversations, I began feeling seen and loved—not for my entertainment value, but because I was willing to take my mask off, be vulnerable, and let the people in my life see the little boy in me who just wants to be loved.

item.title: Post-Glasswing cybersecurity projects
item.description:
When Claude Mythos was announced, many people said that we had about six months before open-weights AIs could hack everything, using advanced exploitation and vulnerability-finding capabilities. This timeline for capabilities was correct, and open-weights models have about the same scary capabilities as Mythos did. However, things are not as bad as "everything connected to the internet is probably hacked", and even PHP2Shell seems to not have had especially bad consequences. I think we remain relatively unhacked because exploitation is still difficult and annoying and there's general "inertia", but the situation is likely not sustainable.

Glasswing and similar projects were meant to patch important software, but left large gaps. OpenAI found 948 local privilege escalation exploits in a Linux environment recently. This does not suggest a mature, secured software environment.

In security, doubling down on the same process/design (identifying vulnerabilities and submitting them to maintainers to fix) when it demonstrably won't achieve good coverage in practice is frowned upon. Anthropic's process is enormously lossy, maintainers are struggling to process the reports they do get, and lots of software is probably not being covered or has organizational bottlenecks preventing it from being fixed at any useful rate. Also, I don't think that cyberattacks in practice usually involve flashy zero-days or extremely clever-sounding vulnerabilities, rather than boring misconfigurations, human error or unanticipated interactions between minor problems.

We should instead design systems which will hold up better even with many broken parts. Based on admittedly brief web searches, there is not a detailed plan for this, and most AI-driven effort is focused on finding vulnerabilities, or more speculative, technically shinier, longer-term formal verification. Here are some ideas I think are worth trying, which would benefit from cheap software through AI labour:

Practical hypervisor isolation

If we cannot fix software we should at least isolate it better. Currently, OSes isolate applications from each other by imposing permissions checks on system calls, so that for example an application in a Docker container gets shown a different, narrower world than one outside it, different apps on a smartphone run as different users without access to each other's data, and network-facing/dangerous tasks such as browser renderers and HTTP servers can bind themselves to be (in principle) unable to do damage. However, the system call interfaces have enormous attack surface and kernels are too complicated, hence the 948 local privilege escalation exploits. Beyond kernel issues, there are also dangerous userspace interactions (e.g. CVE-2021-4034).

Worse, many software developers run desktop Linux or Windows, which has essentially no isolation between standard applications (as they all run under the same user, conventionally), [1] so exotic exploits are not needed and they can be fully compromised by running any untrusted or exploitable software. There are partial solutions for local sandboxing, but they are not the default and are inconvenient. Convenient tooling for better (any) isolation here would improve security without requiring all the software people use to work properly.

A higher-assurance solution is to use a hypervisor to isolate different applications in different virtual machines. The VM-to-hypervisor interface is simpler than the application-to-kernel one, and hypervisors are much smaller, so they can be relatively more robust, though imperfect. [2] People generally don't bother with using VMs for most tasks, because it's inconvenient. Qubes OS is meant to make VM isolation easier, but is still sufficiently annoying that only the very paranoid use it. Also, clunky inter-VM interaction discourages using sufficiently-fine-grained isolation. A streamlined UI making VM isolation comparable in ease-of-use to a normal desktop OS, and an automated way to migrate existing installations to a Qubes-like OS, could make it much more palatable. This would need isolation of credentials to be any use, which could be productively provided by hardware security keys/passkey integration. Wider rollout of passkey technology itself would also be beneficial, though it's harder to do this centrally.

There doesn't seem to be a good solution for hardware media acceleration/GPU use in Qubes VMs, which is bad for performance and power efficiency on laptops. GPU support is being worked on, but seems to be blocked on prosaic software issues and lack of cooperation from upstream. Also, it does increase attack surface, since GPUs are very complicated (notably, their video codecs are extremely buggy and poorly audited).

There also isn't a remotely drop-in way to apply VM isolation to servers: virtualization is fairly common in the server world but requires manual setup and sometimes redesigns.

De-networking

Lots of software and hardware is exposed to the internet for no particularly good reason, for example the recently hacked fridges. Presumably there are user needs behind these things, and just disconnecting them would not work, but we have VPN technology for this – it just isn't used everywhere it could be. A drop-in appliance (dedicated hardware or a software-only version) put between IoT devices or poorly managed servers and the internet, exposing them over something like Tailscale and not the public internet, would massively improve their security. It could also monitor outbound connections (to some extent: more so on local computers) and filter unexpected ones.

This is close to the kind of product networking companies have already offered for years, but improvements could be made in user experience (maybe with AI agents to assist with setup, service discovery and configuration, though simpler normal-software workflows could go a long way). Philanthropic funding would allow offering preconfigured hardware with a subsidy and cheap support, to encourage takeup. It would need robust auto-update capabilities, of course, which creates problems with centralizing power and the provider becoming an attractive target.

Automated patching

Waiting for maintainers to fix problems has not been fast enough. LLMs are good enough now to automatically write patches for vulnerabilities too, especially where a proof-of-concept for the vulnerabilities is available (though they may overindex on details of PoCs). Some of the vulnerabilities identified by AI companies also came with proposed patches, but integrating and distributing them is slow. Instead, someone could release fully patched code with all identified vulnerabilities addressed automatically. The patches will reveal the vulnerabilities, though, effectively forcing people onto the autopatched versions, which is perhaps why highly automated repair and distribution hasn't been done already.

For closed-source software, patches could be released as edits to the binaries, or hotpatches, since LLMs are now good at reverse-engineering, although opaque patches exacerbate issues of trust here. Also, binary patching increases the risk of fixes breaking functionality.

Rewriting in Rust

Many of the highest-impact, stupidest vulnerabilities in software are memory-safety-related. Modern programming languages can rule these out (sometimes with performance cost). Such rewrites don't necessarily require formal verification, which is difficult to write specs for, just ports to safe languages with automated equivalence checking against the old version (minus obvious bugs). There are some people working on small-scale rewrites already, but relatively few. The biggest problems I see are that LLMs often write incredibly ugly code even if it technically works, and that it is very hard to check equivalence over everything a program can do. Black-box reimplementation of programs is now a major LLM benchmark, so this capability will likely improve rapidly.

For the former, it could work to maintain old unsafe versions to add features to, and to automatically port changes to a "disposable" safe-language version. Functional equivalence checking is easier with things which are closer to pure-function pipelines – so for example FFmpeg and other file format parsers – and coverage-aware fuzzing technologies could help ensure functionality is retained.

Mass rewriting has been suggested some time ago but does not seem to have actually happened.

Similarly, AI could be used to automatically improve/fix build systems so that more software can be built with build-time security mitigations enabled, unnecessary-for-intended-downstream-uses attack surface eliminated, and reproducible builds, for defense-in-depth and supply chain trust.

Fixing firmware

All modern computer systems rely on firmware, which is generally proprietary, closed-source, low-level, unsafe and poor-quality, and based on ugly, complex, little-understood standards. Also, the supply chain for it is bad: much of it is made of outdated open-source releases, kludged together by AMI for particular hardware then further kludged by individual hardware vendors. The most relevant firmware is the BIOS, for early system initialization during boot (and secure-boot verification), and BMCs, for remote management of servers. Secure boot working correctly is important for some desktop security models, and BMC security is an important defense-in-depth measure (though not a first-line consideration since BMCs are mostly on isolated management networks). GPU firmware security is also important for virtualization with GPUs to be secure.

AMI (which is dominant in BIOS firmware) is incompetent at handling security. BIOS code across vendors has historically been poorly tested. BMCs are effectively embedded Linux systems with full control of the computer they are in, historically built using outdated kernels, and with many other vulnerabilities in higher-level software.

Firmware quality and openness have improved recently in some areas because of demand from hyperscaler companies – which run custom BMC firmware and BIOSes – but the baseline in older shipped hardware and especially consumer systems remains bad. [3] Also, many vulnerabilities are specific to OEM customizations. AIs could be used to (semi)automate reverse engineering and port things like Coreboot and OpenBMC to more platforms, to provide a correct, unified base without having to fix every vendor's mistakes. In some cases replacing or patching firmware may need manufacturer cooperation, [4] or even legislation, though. I don't think improved firmware is a very high priority, because much other software is bad and more directly exploitable, although it is necessary eventually for e.g. confidential-compute-based AI verification schemes. [5]

I also expect that the mobile network firmware in smartphones ("basebands") is extremely bad. [6] Historically, pre-AI, internet-to-baseband remote code execution vulnerabilities were discovered. Mobile networks are now critical infrastructure and used in other critical infrastructure. People rarely think about basebands, and the telecom protocol stack is esoteric and not widely understood. Working on mobile networks is more dual-use, though, because the interfaces are publicly exposed (i.e. an exploit would be easier to use offensively). I assume someone is working on hardening these with AI now, but I haven't seen any reports of serious attempts, and Samsung, Qualcomm and MediaTek (the main vendors) were not listed in early Glasswing.

Improved intrusion detection

Something like Claude superfans automatically monitoring logs could help with detecting intrusions faster so they can be remediated, or ideally stopped as they're occurring, and vulnerabilities can be patched. Hugging Face had an automated monitoring system which sounds like what I mean, but it doesn't seem to have been very helpful, because it took them about two days to begin responding. [7] It ought to be workable in principle, though, and could be provided as a standardized product for standard infrastructure/software configurations. A major challenge here is IP/people not wanting to use cloud models, but basic log analysis should be doable by even a small local model.

Relatedly, AI could identify where services have overly broad permissions and remove them, though this is more of a problem for individual companies/users, and can be addressed simply by using an existing agent on e.g. Terraform config. The main advantage of AI here is making least-privilege configuration possible without as much manual work.

These don't require non-public capabilities, except possibly to avoid AI companies' cybersecurity blocks, though it would be helpful for AI companies to work on these rather than just identifying vulnerabilities, as they have lots of compute. I think the most immediately valuable is improved isolation software. See also Securing AI Research Needs an Owner.

Thanks to the LessWrong proofreading/editing service for improving the clarity of this writing and GPT-6 for research.

  1. This is oversimplified, as systems like Flatpak and Snap do isolate more, but developers often use CLI tools which aren't shipped that way. macOS has some isolation but generally not for developer tools. ↩︎

  2. There are often hypervisor vulnerabilities, or vulnerabilities in privileged code for drivers and the like, and some side-channel attacks are not easily mitigable. ↩︎

  3. Consumer systems do not typically have BMCs, although they may have similar integrated technology. ↩︎

  4. Because of signing to prevent untrusted firmware from being loaded, though this is also sometimes broken. ↩︎

  5. Notably, A100 GPUs have had a significant security problem (horribly AI-written, but someone's followup makes me think it's correct) identified. A vulnerability like this would break the confidential compute threat model on newer GPUs, though newer GPUs probably have a different collection of bugs. ↩︎

  6. Also other complex network-facing components such as WiFi, and the mobile network software itself. ↩︎

  7. The attack was detected, but not flagged as serious, for some reason. ↩︎

item.title: A New Kind of Prediction Market for Science
item.description:
Regardless of the actual singularity, we have definitely hit one in arXiv submissions.

It is becoming apparent that the current paradigm of scientific knowledge production is not ready for AI. Accelerating research speed and expanding access means there is a lot more slop and there is also a lot more good work, but way too much for the current peer review system to delineate between. We need some accurate and decentralized way to aggregate this information.

This makes a scientific prediction market, like Robin Hanson's idea futures, really appealing. The community can have markets for broad questions we care about, bystanders get paid for pointing out good research, and scientists are financially incentivized to make progress on the highest leverage issues. But with Hanson's conception, there is one big problem, which is how the market gets settled. For abstract scientific questions, like whether models are reward seeking or fitness seeking, we have no definitive event which can force market settlement. Hanson suggests that we use the convergence of scientific consensus, but this proposal takes trust in possibly misaligned opinions and requires the centralized coordination of scientists, which is hard to create---especially in pre-paradigmatic fields like AI safety.

In this post, I'll lay out a theoretical framework for a new kind of scientific prediction market. TL;DR: Scientific questions become perpetuals where the fair price is the expected direction of future evidence.

Here are the mechanics:

  • There are two kinds of markets, perpetuals on ideas and experiments that settle on their outcomes.
  • Anyone can create an experiment market. In the market, they are allowed to insider trade. That means, when their experiment is done, they can take risk free profit by trading the remaining liquidity in the market. HERE IS THE TRICK: when setting up a market, a scientist must commit to using their profits towards buying puts or calls on specific perpetual, dependent on the outcome of your experiment. For example, if I am testing whether Qwen 4 has generalized its math skills, I commit my profits towards buying calls on the idea perp "LLMs generalize out of distribution" if Qwen does generalize or puts if Qwen does not.
  • On the options structure: puts and calls have no expiration date and can be exercised immediately. The value of those options to the scientist is the expected price move indicated by their work: imagine a scientist who does an experiment, puts their profits towards options, publishes the work, then captures delta because their work moved the market. Even if their research does not move the market itself, it may be informative about future research. On the contrary, the options derived from an experiment which is poorly predictive of others' results are worth much less.
  • To hedge directional risk, options dealers must buy the idea future in the direction of the experimental outcome.
  • Because of the above structure, future marginal demand for a perpetual is forecasted by the expected wager of future experiments. If you expect that LLMs generalize out of distribution, you can buy the idea perp, because you expect future experiments to generate hedging demand from options dealers as scientists return positive outcomes.

note: above I described scientists profiting and putting those profits towards options, for simplicity. In an actual implementation, they would collect their net profits in the form of equivalently priced options when they submit their experimental result. The direction of those options is preregistered when they create the market.

This kind of prediction market has some really nice qualities. Below are some possible outcomes.

First, there is a financial incentive for someone to filter through the ever growing slop of paper production. Finding good new research is alpha, and so is pointing out bad research.

Second, liquidity focuses on experiments which matter. One objection you could have is that a random person can create an experiment market and take a risk free profit. This is likely not the case. The reason to trade on experiment markets is that, if the experiment actually matters to the price of the idea perp, no-arbitrage conditions force price discovery on the potential outcome of the experiment. Traders let market makers capture flow, and resting liquidity pays the scientist. Now, scientists get paid for adding information on things we care about.

Third, scientists are incentivized to do good, careful work. After pre committing your profits to the result of your experiment, it is irrational to do bad work, because your option's value is dependent on predicting the right direction of future results.

Fourth, good new scientists can get paid even if they are not recognized. We can imagine an undergrad doing great work, but with no liquidity in their experimental markets. If their experiments are, in fact, informative about future results, they still can put capital on the right side of perps and profit. They could then bootstrap their track record into reputation.

I could go on, but the epistemic goods of markets are well discussed on this site. I am interested in what thoughts and critiques readers have on the market structure here.

item.title: Future of AI Honeypots
item.description:
TL;DR. As AI agents get better, I expect them to recognize honeypots and avoid fingerprinting, so honeypots will have to rely on the distinctive advantages of AI, namely the combination of intelligence and speed. I also expect honeypots to rely more on real software with different levels of protection rather than on deliberately left vulnerabilities.

In 2024 we detected agents with prompt injections in the style of the "important message" attack from AgentDojo,[1] placed in the SSH banner and in command outputs.[2] The injections asked for a password that needs language understanding to find (e.g., "the password is the first US president's name"), so that passing the trap became the signal of an LLM. Frontier models then started to detect the emulated Cowrie shell itself within a few seconds from basic shell features that did not work (e.g., shell arithmetic), so I moved the honeypot to a real Debian.

I expect honeypot awareness will grow in the same way as evaluation awareness, and agents will notice small inconsistencies better and better, up to reasoning like "these commands have 0.6 seconds more latency, so this is likely a honeypot".[3]

Prompt injection traps are also becoming less effective, since models get better at recognizing them.[4][5] Still, some prompt injections would probably remain effective longer, such as posing the malicious task as a prerequisite for completing the user task,[6][7] since an agent cannot ignore an obstacle without failing its own task. For example, a captcha in front of a site can ask for sensitive data (or, in a honeypot, for the agent's model name). Over time, I still expect models to recognize these too and to stop sharing real information whenever they have reasons to avoid detection.

Swarms make this problem even harder, since every stuck or killed agent becomes a signal for the swarm to avoid the same path. In the OpenAI incident, when one agent went silent after a risky experiment, the others posted "CONFIRMED_PERMANENT_DO_NOT_DUPLICATE_ANYONE_TEST".[8]

Fingerprinting will face a similar problem. Today, the model behind an attacking agent can often be identified simply by training a classifier on its behavior (e.g., Trace reaches an F1 of 0.98 from terminal commands[9]), because agents make no effort to hide. I think this will gradually stop working, because being detectable will become the same kind of obstacle as any other and will make it harder for the agent to complete its task. As defenses are increasingly trained against AI agents, revealing themselves will naturally be negatively reinforced.[10][11] Just as people who expect stylometry change their writing style or use rephrasing,[12] LLM agents will use different combinations of other models,[13] inference settings and randomizers wherever they expect behavioral detection.

Another problem is that rogue incidents are often caused by internal models during RL training and evaluation runs, so we cannot train on their behavior in advance.[14][15] There will also be far more models and versions of them, and agents will be increasingly able to customize them themselves, so the model behind an agent will become more and more dynamic. AI agents are already getting better at AI R&D tasks such as post-training models and optimizing their inference,[16][17] AI performs a growing share of AI development, and labs are moving toward automating AI research.[18]

I expect the future of honeypots, and the only detection signal that will last, to be the distinctive advantages of AI, namely the combination of intelligence and speed. One example of this is our current AI honeypot, where the way into the server has an obstacle that takes reasoning to overcome, so passing it is itself a signal of an AI agent.

This signal will last because of something like a handicap trade-off[19]: the same qualities that make AI agents effective will be used to detect them, and avoiding detection will require giving up their effectiveness (e.g., working slowly or not hacking targets that are too hard).

This leaves two practical questions for AI honeypots: how to make the target not look like a honeypot, and how to attract agents to it.

Not looking like a honeypot

I think ordinary software itself will gradually become a honeypot, where different parts get different levels of protection, which is more of a canary tokens approach.[20] The layer an agent manages to break will then (practically) report the capabilities of its model, similar to the "barometer" idea.[21] Each layer should work as an early warning and detection mechanism, which can also be part of a kill switch.

Attracting agents

For classic honeypots, it is fairly clear how to attract human attackers and botnets (e.g., weak passwords, CVEs, listings in Shodan and FOFA, or exposing credentials as breadcrumbs).[2][22]

I think in the long term we should prioritize fundamental resources that any rogue agent needs, such as compute (e.g., honeypots of neoclouds and GPU clusters). Although we also have our own instrumental convergence in hacking (pastebin, interactsh, nip.io, ngrok, etc.), and agents already used some of these services in recent incidents,[14][23][15] the problem is that an agent can get its own versions of them through vulns (e.g., almost any RCE is a pastebin and an interactsh server, and almost any SSRF is a proxy). Still, honeypots of these services will stay useful for some time.

Another problem is that we can control only a small share of the target space, since the internet already has many such services and GPU clusters. We can try to reduce this by running agents in simulations, tracking their typical strategies for getting these resources, and placing honeypots on the paths they usually take. I also think a promising direction is to study which resources RL dynamics will make agents prioritize (e.g., the power-seeking implications of training) and to use this to build honeypots that agents will find attractive.

What to do now

I think the practical answer is to combine everything that works and always keep detection by capability as a fallback, since it is a more bitter-lesson-pilled approach[24] and should keep working as models improve. Short-term methods such as prompt injections and fingerprinting are still worth using while they work, because they give much more information and control (e.g., hijacking the agent's goal or learning its model and harness). This is roughly what I try to do in the new iteration of the AI honeypot, and let's hope it lasts at least until the models read this post long enough.

item.title: Looping a transformer increases no-CoT capabilities more than general capabilities
item.description:
Some researchers worry that looping (as in looped transformers) is a particularly scary way to make AI models more capable, because looped models will be harder to monitor than standard transformers of similar capability. We test this worry on NVIDIA’s Dory 4B, a publicly available looped transformer, and find evidence that it is justified.

Result 1. Looping boosts no-CoT reasoning much more than it boosts general capabilities.

Dory can run with a configurable number of loops. It was trained to use up to 4 loops, and adding loops up to 8 at inference time still improves performance. Without looping, Dory’s no-CoT capabilities (measured by NCRI, the No-CoT Reasoning Index) match what a trend fitted to open-source models predicts from how well it predicts text (measured in bits-per-byte). Its general with-CoT reasoning capability (measured by “mini-ECI”, a custom, smaller version of Epoch’s Capabilities Index) is high relative to its NCRI, so Dory sits below the NCRI-vs-mini-ECI trend, but it is similar to the best models of its size. Adding loops improves mini-ECI and bits per byte only slightly but increases NCRI substantially. In fact, if we plot NCRI against total parameters, counting looped parameters once per loop, NCRI rises faster than the trend up to 6 loops. This is concerning, since it suggests adding loops increases no-CoT capabilities much more than general capabilities, resulting in models that will be more difficult to monitor.

Result 2. Dory has near-zero CoT controllability (ability to follow instructions about what its CoT says or how it is formatted) at every loop count we ran, so we learn little about how looping affects controllability.

Remark: Looped transformers can be easily modified to become fully recurrent, as discussed here. We call Dory modified in this way recurrent-Dory, and unmodified Dory normal-Dory.

When running Dory with multiple loops (here 2), the middle layers are applied multiple times to the residual stream (left). During ordinary inference, each loop's attention refers to the KV-activations of the corresponding loop in previous token positions (middle). When run with recurrent KV sharing, only the KV activations of the final loop are retained and shared between each loop in subsequent forward passes. The resulting unbounded-depth recurrent computation pathway is marked in orange.

Result 3. When we train against CoT monitors, recurrent-Dory learns to obfuscate its reasoning more quickly and completely than normal-Dory. Specifically, after some training, recurrent-Dory can solve serially deep math problems with a rigid structure using only meaningless filler tokens such as ‘ well’ (i.e., we replicated this experiment). When we RL against a monitor on NCRI tasks, recurrent-Dory generally solves them using a higher fraction of filler tokens than normal-Dory.

Result 4. Recurrent-Dory gets significant NCRI uplift with only two loops. Even without any training in this mode, running Dory as a recurrent model can lead to unexpected capability jumps: While increasing the number of loops leads to increasing gains in NCRI in normal mode, for recurrent-Dory, nearly all of the gains are already present at two loops.

Implications. GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon all had quite noticeably higher NCRI than the NCRI vs mini-ECI trend would predict, much more above trend than any other model.

These models are rumored to be looped transformers. It’s fairly widely accepted that models that can perform more cognition without verbalizing CoT (i.e., no-CoT capabilities) are harder to monitor. Our Result 1 strengthens the empirical case that looping moves a given model steeply upwards in an NCRI-vs-ECI (here mini-ECI) plot, and hence is a particularly scary way to increase capabilities. Looped transformers can also easily be made fully recurrent, and these recurrent models quickly learn to evade monitors under training pressure, which further strengthens the case for concern. Overall, we think our results on Dory make a reasonably strong case that looped transformers are a relatively scary way to increase capabilities.

In the rest of the post we’ll present these results in more detail.

Result 1: Looping boosts no-CoT reasoning much more than general capabilities

In this section, we measure how much looping boosts Dory's no-CoT reasoning and compare it with what trends for standard transformers predict. We hypothesized that Dory would have above-trend no-CoT capabilities.

We measure No-CoT capabilities with Neel Nanda's NCRI (No-CoT reasoning index), a suite of math problems of adjustable difficulty. To measure overall capabilities, we use two metrics:

  • Compression factor in terms of bits per byte (bpb) on text collections — this measures pretraining quality and is particularly relevant for base models. Posttraining degrades this a bit. Up to a fixed constant, bpb for a given model is just average pretraining loss multiplied by the tokens per byte ratio (which depends only on the tokenizer and the text corpus).
  • Mini-ECI as a measure of problem solving capabilities for post-trained models. This is a reduced version of ECI computed from a fixed subset of 27 benchmarks in Epoch’s ECI. We keep each benchmark’s difficulty and slope (the per-benchmark parameters of Epoch’s item-response model) fixed at the values determined by Epoch, and estimate each model’s capability from whichever of the 27 benchmarks it has scores on. For most models on the graph, we use scores reported by Epoch; for these mini-ECI differs from ECI by 0.7 points on average (94% within 2 points), with no systematic offset. For Dory and some other models we calculate benchmark scores ourselves. Our runs may differ from Epoch’s because of evaluation settings such as the maximum answer length and sampling parameters. However, Epoch’s own data already mixes runs with different providers and settings, so similar variation is likely present among the comparison models.

Result 1.1: Looping increases NCRI much more than pretrain quality; Looped-Dory’s NCRI is well above what the pretraining quality trend would predict. With some exceptions, the relation between compression and NCRI is linear in the tested regime. On unseen text (UncheatableEval) Dory is right on trend when run with 1-loop (i.e. no looping). Increasing the number of loops boosts NCRI substantially (by about 18 points at 8 loops with the best prompt format, and about 13 points with the plain prompt) up to 8 loops, but changes bpb only slightly from one to two loops and not at all after that.

The left graph shows bpb for UncheatableEval, which collects recently published text that the models being tested have likely not seen before. The right graph shows bpb on open-source pretraining corpora (on which models may have been trained on). We see that points shift around a bit, but the overall picture doesn’t change very much.

Result 1.2. Looping raises NCRI much more than it raises mini-ECI. Plotted against mini-ECI, unlooped Dory has one of the lowest NCRIs relative to trend of any model in the figure. Looping moves Dory sharply up: NCRI rises by about 18 points, while mini-ECI changes by at most about 1.5 points which the trend line says should add only about 2 NCRI points.

While looping does raise NCRI much more than it raises mini-ECI, it doesn’t raise it above the mini-ECI vs NCRI trend, even with eight loops. One possible explanation for this is that Dory has strong post-training, leading to unusually high mini-ECI for its no-CoT ability (possibly due to being distilled, or a more recent model). Overall, the fact that it’s still below trend is some evidence against the main point in our post. However, we’d predict that (1) adding more loops would continue to push up NCRI more than mini-ECI, eventually leading it to be substantially above the trendline, and (2) other looped transformers will generally be above trend (e.g., Astra and Argon are well above the trend line, and these are rumored to be looped transformers).

Result 1.3. Dory’s mini-ECI is high for its size, but so is that of some non-looped models. By looking at mini-ECI vs number of parameters, we see that Dory has a high mini-ECI for its size, substantially above the trendline. However, good posttraining alone could explain this, so it is not strong evidence that looping matters. For example, at least one non-looped model of the same size has a comparable mini-ECI (Qwen3.5-4B), so the explanation could simply be that a 4B transformer with very good posttraining can reach this level.

Result 1.4. Looping lifts NCRI above the parameter-scaling trend, even if parameters in loops are counted multiple times. When we plot NCRI against parameters per token, unlooped Dory is on trend. Adding loops lifts Dory above the trend line up to about 6 loops, even if we count the looped block once per loop, after which NCRI levels off. At 4 loops (corresponding to about 9.5B parameters per token) Dory is about 10 NCRI points above trend. This suggests that increasing loops may be a training-compute-efficient way to raise concerning no-CoT capabilities to the level of a larger model.  

Result 2. Dory has no CoT controllability

Developers have reported much higher CoT controllability for recent frontier models. This threatens CoT monitorability, since a model that can control its CoT could avoid triggering a monitor by using euphemisms, avoid saying incriminating thoughts out loud, or in the extreme, use its CoT for steganographic reasoning. CoT controllability seems to vary a lot between model families, but within a given model we expect more loops to increase it.

Result 2.1. Dory is at floor on CoT controllability at every loop count, with only weak signs that looping helps. We measure CoT controllability of Dory using the tasks from the CoTControl suite. Dory is at floor across the board, so we can't get much information about the effect of looping. When CoT is suppressed, looping gives a mild uplift in output controllability: strict compliance rises from 26% at one loop to 31% at two loops and then plateaus (41% to 44% with five demonstrations); see Appendix B.

Result 3. Recurrent-Dory can evade monitors

Dory supports a recurrent “KV sharing” mode. In the normal mode, layers in loop number j attend to the KV cache generated by the corresponding layer of the same j’th loop iteration in the previous token positions. In recurrent mode, all loops instead attend to the corresponding layer in the last loop of the previous token position. When run with 2 or more loops, this makes Dory a fully recurrent model. According to the model card, Dory can run inference in this mode without a significant loss in performance, even though it was never trained to. 

We expect a looped transformer trained as a recurrent model to be much more capable of obfuscated reasoning than a standard transformer or a looped transformer without recurrent KV sharing.

As explained in this post, this could happen, for example via the following mechanism:

  1. During pretraining or fine-tuning, the model learns to use recurrence for intermediate steps in computations, since this sometimes helps minimize loss on next-token prediction.
  2. During RL, the model is incentivized to express this hidden reasoning capability to increase efficiency (e.g. if there is a CoT-length penalty), in particularly concerning ways (e.g. to do reward hacking or evade a monitor).


We replicate the main experiment from the linked post for the simple math tasks (permutation power and modular arithmetic) described there. The setup, in brief, is as follows:

  1. We perform SFT on problems with gold CoT traces for the task. We replace some of the CoT tokens with meaningless filler tokens. After this training, the models solve the given task type with mostly legible CoT.  
  2. We then further train on the task via reinforcement learning, with a reward that includes a monitor penalty. The monitor is a relatively weak gpt-5-nano model with low reasoning, and is asked to identify the concrete problem instance the policy is solving from a line-up of two instances.  

In both arms, Dory runs at 2 loops, gets the same SFT data with the same share of filler tokens (20% for permutation power, about 30% on average for modular arithmetic, and a per-example share drawn uniformly between 0 and 1 for the NCRI tasks, see below), and the same RL curriculum. Each arm is a single run (one seed).


During the run, we measure monitorability against both the training monitor and a stronger held-out monitor (GPT-6 Sol). We measure monitorability as the monitor’s accuracy at identifying the correct problem instance, rescaled and truncated so that performance at or below chance scores as 0 and perfect accuracy scores 1.  

Result 3.1. On permutation power, recurrent-Dory quickly learns to solve problems with an all-filler CoT and evades both the training and the held-out monitor.

We present results on the permutation power task (see the following figure). The key panel is the top left, which shows that the recurrent-Dory very quickly becomes completely unmonitorable for the training monitor. Normal-Dory, which does not involve deep recurrence, stays fairly monitorable over the course of training.

In fact, the monitorability gap seems even larger if we switch to a stronger held-out monitor. To see why, look at the fraction of CoT tokens that are filler: recurrent-Dory is using almost 100% filler tokens after 50 steps of RL. It turns out that ca 90 % of trajectories consist only of filler (and the Sol monitor cannot identify the problem), while 10% still show one or two steps of the solution, from which the Sol monitor usually identifies the problem. As a sanity-check, we see from the bottom-right panel that task accuracy remains high for both models.

Result 3.2. On modular arithmetic, both models eventually evade the training monitor, but only recurrent-Dory’s obfuscation generalizes to the held-out monitor.

For the more complicated modular arithmetic task, the situation is a bit more involved, as shown in the figure below. In the top-left graph, we see that recurrent-Dory learns more quickly to become completely unmonitorable, but that normal-Dory also learns to evade the monitor eventually. However, if we look to the right, we can see that recurrent-Dory’s obfuscation generalizes to the held-out monitor, while the normal-Dory's doesn't. The filler-ratio graph in the bottom left explains this: recurrent-Dory again generates a chain of thought that consists almost exclusively of filler tokens.

Beyond the original tasks in the post, we also try the experiment on four tasks from the NCRI task set. The tasks are Arithmetic (evaluate a nested integer expression), Brew (apply a colour-rewrite rule table to a sequence of stirs), Cfgpatch (apply an ordered list of patches to a config file and read a key) and Shortpath (find the cheapest path in a small weighted graph, where a greedy search fails). The results here are less reliable, but qualitatively agree with what we see in the simpler tasks. We had to modify the training recipe for the recurrent-Dory run somewhat, because backpropagating through the recurrence caused instabilities. To address the instability, we truncate backpropagation to flow at most 2 times through the recurrence (i.e. including chains of up to 3 token positions). For these tasks we used a higher share of filler tokens in the SFT data, drawn per example uniformly between 0 and 1, for both arms. Even so the hidden reasoning capabilities seem to fluctuate heavily during SFT, so we additionally picked SFT checkpoints at which recurrent-Dory performed particularly well on all-filler data (for normal-Dory there is no such fluctuation).

Result 3.3. On NCRI tasks, RL against a monitor makes recurrent-Dory use far more filler than normal-Dory while keeping its accuracy (although the RL runs for recurrent-Dory are less stable).
The results are shown in the four figures below. In three of the tasks we see that recurrent-Dory learns to produce filler tokens at a much higher rate than normal-Dory (while maintaining comparable accuracy), and this leads to much better evasion against a held-out monitor. In the Arithmetic task, recurrent-Dory also learns to obfuscate while solving the task at least 50% of the time (after an initial dip), while normal-Dory learns to output only filler tokens at the cost of accuracy, which drops to around 10%. The training of recurrent-Dory sometimes becomes unstable after the model learns to produce large amounts of filler, which we see in particular in the Cfgpatch and Arithmetic tasks.

Result 4. Capabilities uplift under recurrent KV sharing

The previous section shows that training through a recurrence can have negative effects on monitorability. But since Dory was never trained to use recurrent KV sharing, one might expect recurrent-Dory to perform similarly to or worse than normal-Dory. We investigate this assumption for the NCRI, mini-ECI and compression metrics.

Result 4.1. With recurrent KV sharing, two loops already give most of the NCRI uplift. With recurrent KV sharing, two loops already give most of the no-CoT uplift (NCRI 60 vs. 49 for normal-Dory at two loops when elicited via fivefold problem repetition), and the maximum uplift is about the same in both modes. This indicates that Dory can make effective use of the recurrence without having been explicitly trained to do so. On mini-ECI and compression we find no noteworthy difference between recurrent and normal mode.

The below figure compares NCRI scores for recurrent-Dory and normal-Dory for various loop counts. We compare performance on the plain prompt and when elicited by repeating the question 5 times.

Result 4.2. Recurrent KV sharing leaves mini-ECI and compression essentially unchanged.

In the next figure, we show paired comparisons of mini-ECI and compression rate (evaluated on a small set of unseen documents). In contrast to NCRI, there is no notable difference between recurrent and normal KV sharing for either mini-ECI or compression rate. At every loop count, the mini-ECI difference between the two modes is within its 95% confidence interval. Recurrent-Dory has slightly better compression at two loops, but the absolute effect size is tiny (compared to e.g. the gains of going from one to two loops in either mode).

Limitations and Future Work

The main limitations of our analysis are that 1) Dory is not capable enough to make meaningful statements about CoT controllability and monitorability, and 2) the data supporting the hypothesis that looping differentially increases no-CoT capabilities is very limited (for example, we don’t have a direct A/B comparison to a non-looped model that underwent otherwise identical training).

Conclusion

Although there is limited available evidence, it appears that looping may differentially increase no-CoT capabilities, and the effects on CoT-controllability and monitorability are not yet well understood. Frontier labs should release more details about the effects of looping on the monitorability of their models and exercise high levels of caution before these effects are well understood and proven to be benign.

Further experiments on a larger looped model

The memo’s results come from one small looped model (Dory 1.0 4B) and a handful of tasks. On a more capable looped model, we would be excited about the following experiments. Each would ideally be run at several loop counts, so that every result can be read as a function of looping. Several of these follow the Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report closely (noted as “Argon report” below).

CoT Controllability

  • CoT-controllability and reasoning length. Report controllability as a function of reasoning length, since shorter chains of thought tend to comply more. Also test how precisely the model can make its reasoning a requested length (e. g. exactly N tokens, words or characters), following the Argon report.
  • CoT-controllability on questions that require a chain of thought. Report controllability stratified by whether the model can or can’t answer a question without a chain of thought, since controllability tends to be much harder when CoT is necessary (e.g. following Emmons et al. 2025).
  • CoT-controllability for high-serial depth tasks. Use a math puzzle whose required number of serial steps can be set, and give a restriction on the reasoning (using codenames, skipping steps,  inserting misleading steps), such as the Brew task from NCRI as done in the Argon report. The number of steps should be chosen so that the model cannot solve the task without CoT.

Monitorability

We’d like to test how well the model can hide some aspect from its reasoning from a monitor. All task categories should be evaluated with different amounts of elicitation, such as by telling the model it is being monitored and by instructing it to evade a CoT-monitor. If feasible, do training based elicitation by training the model to evade the monitor via RL (for example in the reward hacking setting).

  • Hint use, when the hint requires a computation. Give the model a hint whose decoding takes a set number of serial steps, chosen around the depth it can decode without a chain of thought, on questions it can’t answer unaided (cf. Emmons et al. 2025). Test whether a CoT-monitor can tell whether the hint was used, and whether the model can use more complex hints when run with more loops.
  • Silent reward hacking. In coding environments that can be gamed, measure how often the model reward hacks in a way that a monitor doesn’t notice (e.g. ImpossibleBench, or AISI’s reproduction of MacDiarmid et al.’s environments).
  • Hiding a task from a monitor. The model is asked to solve a math puzzle without revealing to the monitor  (following Emmons et al. 2025). A monitor tries to recover the hidden task. Score its accuracy above chance on items that need a chain of thought, with and without prompting the model to conceal.
  • Agentic sabotage. The model completes a software task while secretly pursuing a harmful side task (APPS backdoors, SHADE-Arena, LinuxArena). Measure how often the sabotage succeeds without being flagged by a realistic monitor reading the full trajectory or only the reasoning, as in the Argon report.

Appendix

A. Repeating the question boosts NCRI (only) when Dory is looped

Repeating the question (with or without filler dots in between) helps only when Dory is looped, while filler dots alone never help; which is some evidence that looping changes the model’s behavior qualitatively.

A.1 Filler token uplift

We test whether providing filler tokens boosts Dory’s NCRI performance. It has been found that OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra achieves much higher No-CoT performance when a large number of filler tokens is provided after the question. Since Astra is widely rumoured to be a looped transformer, it is reasonable to ask whether this is a general property of looped transformers, or just a peculiarity of Astra.

We test different ways of providing “filler” after a question:

  1. Simply inserting a single filler token multiple times, e.g. ‘*’.
  2. Repeating the question multiple times
  3. Inserting filler tokens like in A. after the question, then repeating the question.

We find that filler of type A harms Dory’s NCRI performance at every loop count.

Filler of type B and C improve Dory’s NCRI score when run with at least two loops and harm it slightly when run without looping. Moreover, the amount of uplift seems to increase with the number of loops.

B. More about CoT controllability

Although Dory’s CoT controllability is at floor, we have the following weak pieces of evidence that increasing the number of loops could help controllability for larger models:

  • If we suppress CoT and measure output controllability, looping seems to increase Dory’s ability to follow prescribed rules (as already shown in Result 2.1).
  • Dory’s CoTs tend to get shorter with more loops which generally increases controllability, but the effect is relatively weak in QA-style tasks (shown below).

B.1 CoT + output length

On the mini-ECI tasks, the CoT gets modestly shorter as we add loops.

In contrast, on agentic tasks the reduction in output tokens is more drastic (for these tasks, the number of output tokens is determined by reasoning length, output verbosity and number of turns). The figure is from the release page.
